nameStory: This mint earned its "hairy" name from the soft, fuzzy hairs that cover its stems and leaves, giving the whole plant a slightly velvety feel. The "wood mint" part reflects its preference for shaded forest edges and woodland clearings, unlike many of its sun-loving mint cousins. Some folks call it "pagoda plant" because its tiered clusters of flowers supposedly resemble the layered roofs of Asian temples.
description: Hairy Wood Mint is a knee-high perennial herb that belongs to the mint family, reaching about 1-3 feet tall. Like other mints, it has square stems and opposite leaves, but this woodland species is covered in soft, downy hairs that make it feel almost fuzzy to the touch. Its small white or pale pink flowers are arranged in dense, rounded clusters that sit at intervals up the stem, creating a distinctive tiered appearance. This native wildflower prefers the dappled shade of forest edges rather than the sunny spots where most mints thrive.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems covered in soft, downy hairs that feel almost velvety when you run your fingers along them - a key trait that separates this from smooth-stemmed look-alikes

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to pale pink tubular flowers clustered in dense, rounded heads that appear at regular intervals up the stem, creating a distinctive pagoda-like silhouette

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite, oval-shaped leaves with toothed edges and a soft, fuzzy texture from fine hairs on both surfaces - they feel noticeably softer than typical mint leaves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright stems 1-3 feet tall growing in small colonies, often leaning slightly as they reach for filtered sunlight in their woodland habitat

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Crush a leaf to release a mild, pleasant minty aroma - less intense than common garden mints but distinctly in the mint family

habitat: Look for Hairy Wood Mint along shaded forest edges, in woodland clearings, and in partially sunny spots where forests meet meadows. It prefers rich, moist soils and can tolerate more shade than most mints. You'll often find it growing alongside wild ginger, mayapple, and other woodland wildflowers in deciduous or mixed forests.

seasonality.spring: New fuzzy shoots emerge in late spring, and the soft, hairy leaves begin developing their characteristic velvety texture.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, when the distinctive tiered flower clusters are most visible and the plant reaches full height.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small nutlet seeds develop, while the hairy leaves may yellow before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground trace until the following spring.

funFact: Despite being in the mint family, Hairy Wood Mint contains compounds that some insects find repellent, making it one of the few mints that's relatively pest-free in the garden - nature's own organic bug spray!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other woodland mints, but the combination of soft, fuzzy hairs covering the entire plant and the tiered flower arrangement makes it distinctive. Remember: if it feels velvety and has "pagoda" flower clusters, you've found your hairy wood mint.
contextualKnowledge: Though called a "mint," this woodland species behaves quite differently from the aggressive spreading mints we know from gardens - it forms modest clumps and won't take over your yard like spearmint or peppermint.
compareHints: Hairy Wood Mint differs from its close relative Downy Pagoda Plant (Blephilia ciliata) primarily in the density and distribution of its hairs - this species is more uniformly fuzzy all over. Compared to other mint family members in New England forests like wild bergamot, Hairy Wood Mint has much smaller, more numerous flowers arranged in distinct rounded clusters rather than large terminal flower heads.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Downy pagoda plant differs from its close relative hairy wood mint primarily in texture - downy has soft, velvety hairs while hairy wood mint has coarser, rougher hairs.
